name: Protein shakes / whey
lead: Whey protein is a mixture of proteins isolated from whey, the liquid left when milk is curdled for cheese, and is sold as a powder that is stirred into water, milk or a blender shake. People use it to reach daily protein targets with little cooking, which supports muscle building and recovery after training and, through that, a more muscular and leaner-looking physique.[1][20]

Whey is among the most widely used supplements in lifting and looksmaxxing circles. Members of looksmax.org discuss whether to start a shake habit, how to reach protein goals when they dislike meat, and which forms to buy.[6][7] It has a place in bodybuilding culture that stretches back to the egg-protein powders of the 1950s and the supplement boom of the 1970s and 1980s.[21]

The research base is large. A 2018 meta-analysis of 49 randomised trials (1,863 participants) found protein supplementation added a small amount of fat-free mass and strength during resistance training, while the International Society of Sports Nutrition describes whey as rapidly digested, leucine-rich and among the most effective protein sources for stimulating muscle protein synthesis.[19][20] The European Food Safety Authority in 2010 found whey about as effective as other protein sources for strength, muscle and lean mass, and found no support for weight-loss claims.[1]

Whey is regulated as a food or dietary supplement in most markets and is a cause of some milk allergies.[1] Product-quality reporting, including protein-spiking investigations and heavy-metal testing of protein powders, is part of the public conversation around it.[21]

paras: Whey is roughly a 5 percent lactose solution that also holds soluble milk proteins and some fat. In cow's milk about 20 percent of the protein is whey and 80 percent casein, and within whey about 65 percent is beta-lactoglobulin, 25 percent alpha-lactalbumin and 8 percent bovine serum albumin.[1]

Concentrate (WPC) keeps some lactose and fat. Isolate (WPI) has most fat and lactose removed and is typically over 90 percent protein by dry weight. Hydrolysate (WPH) is partially pre-digested, costs more, and has smaller peptides that make it less allergenic, which is why it is used in hypoallergenic infant formulas and medical foods. Native whey is taken from skim milk rather than cheese byproduct and so lacks glycomacropeptide, which forms only when rennet is used.[1]

Whey is made mainly by membrane filtration, in which microfiltration removes bacteria, casein micelles and fat and ultrafiltration retains the proteins before spray drying, or by ion-exchange chromatography. Diafiltration, which washes lactose and minerals out during ultrafiltration, made higher-protein concentrates and isolates practical.[1] Industrial reviews discuss quality problems in dried whey powder production such as caking.[8]

Lifters take whey after training or between meals as a convenient protein source. Reference summaries state that post-exercise intake raises free amino acids and supports protein recovery and synthesis, while taking it before exercise does not improve performance on its own.[1] Bodybuilding literature lists whey and casein as common supplements, with experts disagreeing on total protein amounts.[2]

On looksmax.org, one user who has trained for a long time asks if it is time to start shakes; replies say both pre-packaged shakes and powder are fine, and another member says he finds it hard to hit his protein without whey.[6] A different poster who dislikes meat says protein shakes are the only way he consistently gets protein, while another member notes that a soft diet gives the teeth and jaw little to chew.[7]

Whey is used in sports and recovery drinks, meal replacements, medical nutrition and as a thickener in yogurt, and the Wikipedia article says its importance in sports nutrition and weight management grew from the late 1980s.[1] Trials also test it in older adults for muscle function and cognition.[9]

The 2010 EFSA opinion, as summarised in reference sources, found whey roughly as effective as other protein sources for strength, muscle and lean body mass, and found no support for fat-loss or satiety claims.[1] The same sources say whey is more bioavailable than casein or soy protein.[1]

Studies of whey in specific groups include a randomised crossover trial comparing whey, soy and egg white on glycaemia after a second meal in normoglycaemic adults [3], and registered trials of whey shakes and appetite, muscle function and digestion.[4][10][11][12]

The 2018 meta-analysis in the British Journal of Sports Medicine pooled 49 randomised controlled trials with 1,863 participants. Protein supplementation increased fat-free mass by 0.30 kg and one-repetition-maximum strength by 2.49 kg over training alone; the fat-free-mass effect shrank with age and was larger in resistance-trained people (0.75 kg), and total intake above about 1.6 g/kg/day produced no further gains in the analysis.[19]

The International Society of Sports Nutrition's 2017 position stand states that about 1.4 to 2.0 g/kg/day is sufficient for most exercising people to build or maintain muscle, that about 0.25 g/kg or 20 to 40 g of high-quality protein per serving is an effective dose, and that higher intakes (2.3 to 3.1 g/kg/day) may help resistance-trained people keep lean mass while dieting. It describes the benefit of peri-workout timing as smaller when daily protein is already adequate, and reports that pre-sleep casein raised overnight muscle protein synthesis.[20]

Whey proteins cause some milk allergies, although caseins are the major milk allergens, and extensive hydrolysis lowers allergenicity.[1] Lactose in concentrate is a consideration for lactose-intolerant users, and isolate has most lactose removed.[1]

Product quality has also been in the news: a 2026 Hacker News thread discussed a California fitness company allegedly selling cake batter as protein powder.[13] A 2024 paper analysed the composition of protein shakes on the Chilean market.[14]

Contamination and labelling have drawn scrutiny. A 2015 Consumer Reports analysis reported unsafe levels of arsenic, cadmium, lead and mercury in several protein powders it tested, and a 2015 CBC investigation reported that protein spiking, the addition of cheap amino-acid filler to inflate measured protein, was not uncommon; many companies disputed the claims.[21] In the US, supplements are regulated under the Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act of 1994, which shifted responsibility for safety to manufacturers and removed pre-market FDA approval.[21]
Supplement-industry criticism more broadly, including by science communicators, targets poorly regulated products and sponsorship-driven promotion in fitness media.[21]

In the late 1960s whey volumes were an economic and environmental problem for New Zealand's dairy industry. In September 1969 Coca-Cola's Dr Alex Malaspina approached the New Zealand Dairy Board seeking soluble whey protein for acidic carbonated drinks. In September 1970 the Dairy Research Institute produced a 65 percent protein concentrate by ultrafiltration that met the solubility and clarity needs, and in 1971 Coca-Cola launched the whey-fortified orange drink Tai in Brazil.[1]

A US patent covering a whey concentrate for acidic beverages was issued to Malaspina and Roberto Moretti on 22 July 1975. The industry formed the Whey Products Corporation in 1982, and the New Zealand Dairy Board's 2001 merger created Fonterra, a leading supplier. Whey became commercially important in sports nutrition in the late 1980s.[1]

Protein for muscle has a longer lineage than whey. Wikipedia traces it to Eugen Sandow's early-1900s emphasis on diet control, Earle Liederman's beef juice, and egg-based protein powders marketed to bodybuilders by Irvin P. Johnson in the 1950s, followed by rapid growth of the supplement industry in the 1970s and 1980s as whey became commercially important.[21][1]

Lifters and looksmaxxers typically use whey as a convenient way to cover protein while eating in a calorie surplus to build muscle or in a deficit to keep muscle while losing fat. The usual appearance rationale is that more muscle (shoulders, back, arms) improves frame and proportions, while retained muscle during a cut keeps a lean look from tipping into a thin one.[19][20]

Variants discussed include concentrate for price, isolate for people who are sensitive to lactose, casein for pre-sleep use, and plant proteins for people avoiding dairy; the position stand notes whey's faster amino-acid appearance in blood compared with casein.[1][20]

Whey is sold as a dietary supplement across Europe and North America. Bodybuilding culture treats the shake as a staple, and T Nation forum members mention it in diet logs and joke about it.[15] Price increases have drawn comment from members who normally get protein from food.[16] Lemmy users have compared supplement experiences, including one who says some Belgian and Dutch fitness influencers promote expensive pre-workouts.[17]
Looksmax.org threads include jokes, such as a user posting that a 25 lb protein powder shipment arrived and others replying with ironic comments about the quantity.[18]

The largest synthesis is the 2018 meta-analysis of 49 randomised trials showing small average gains in fat-free mass and strength with protein supplementation during resistance training, alongside the International Society of Sports Nutrition's 2017 position stand on protein and exercise.[19][20]

A randomised crossover trial compared whey, soy and egg white protein on blood glucose after a second meal in normoglycaemic adults.[3] Registered trials have examined whey shakes and appetite or energy intake in people with obesity (n=12), and a large program combining exercise and protein supplementation for sarcopenia prevention in older adults (n=801).[4][5] Other registered studies cover whey versus a peptide product on muscle function in older adults (n=81) [10], protein digestion variability (n=18) [11], and exercise-induced gastrointestinal symptoms (n=13) [12]. A 12-month randomised trial tested a whey powder rich in milk fat globule membrane, taurine and B vitamins on cognition in older adults with mild cognitive impairment.[9] No studies were found on whey and facial appearance.

lore.intro: Whey is discussed in looksmaxxing and lifting forums as a practical way to reach protein targets, and sometimes as a joke item.

claims.claim: Protein shakes are a needed way to hit protein for muscle gain
claims.believers: A looksmax.org member says he finds it very hard to hit his protein without whey, and another calls shakes the only way he consistently gets protein.[6][7]
claims.experts: EFSA, as summarised in reference sources, found whey about as effective as other protein sources for strength, muscle and lean mass.[1]

claims.believers: Dieters on forums mention replacing meals with shakes while cutting.[15]
claims.experts: The 2010 EFSA assessment found no evidence supporting weight-loss claims for whey.[1] Small registered trials have studied appetite effects.[4]

claims.claim: A shake-heavy soft diet gives the jaw too little to chew
claims.believers: A looksmax.org reply points out that chewing is good for the jaw and the shake-and-sandwich diet barely uses the teeth.[7]
claims.experts: No studies in this area were found specific to whey shakes and jaw development.

claims.claim: You must eat protein within an anabolic window right after training
claims.believers: Lifters commonly take whey after training, and reference summaries describe post-exercise intake as raising amino acids and supporting protein synthesis.[1]
claims.experts: The International Society of Sports Nutrition says pre- and post-exercise protein both help but that timing benefits appear smaller when total daily protein is adequate.[20]

claims.claim: More protein always means more muscle
claims.believers: Forum culture favours very high intakes and large tubs of powder.[18]
claims.experts: A 2018 meta-analysis found no further fat-free-mass gain from supplementation beyond about 1.6 g/kg/day total protein.[19]

claims.claim: Protein powders can be contaminated or mislabelled
claims.believers: Consumers on fitness forums sometimes question product quality and price.[13][16]
claims.experts: Consumer Reports (2015) reported heavy metals in several powders and a CBC investigation reported protein spiking, which companies disputed.[21]

card.summary: Milk-derived powder for hitting protein targets; about as effective as other protein sources, with no facial-appearance studies.
card.note: Whey is a milk-derived allergen for some people.

quick.overview:
Whey protein is a powder made from the liquid left over in cheese making, mixed into shakes for convenient protein. Lifters and looksmaxxers use it to support muscle gain and body composition.

A 2010 EFSA panel, as summarised in reference sources, found it roughly as effective as other proteins for muscle and strength.
quick.mechanism: Whey supplies amino acids that support muscle protein synthesis, especially after resistance exercise.
quick.risks: Whey can trigger milk allergy in some people. It is sold as a food supplement. Studies specific to appearance were not found.

chain: Easier to reach daily protein targets
Supports muscle protein synthesis after resistance training
More muscle and a leaner-looking frame
angle.text: Whey raises circulating amino acids after a shake, which supports muscle protein synthesis. Lifters use it to fill gaps in their protein intake, and the extra muscle mass and leanness they train for changes how the body looks.
